newsitem.title: CANADA: Hydro-Quebec defends Churchill Falls power pact.
newsitem.headline: Hydro-Quebec defends Churchill Falls power pact.

text.p: Quebec government-owned utility Hydro-Quebec on Tuesday defended the lucrative long-term contract under which it purchases electricity from Newfoundland's Churchill Falls (Labrador) Corp at advantageous rates.
On Monday, Newfoundland Premier Brian Tobin demanded that the contract, which runs to 2041, be renegotiated because Churchill Falls will begin losing money on it in 2001.

Newfoundland contends that the electricity, which amounts to about 30 billion kilowatt hours annually from the 5,420 megawatt facility in Labrador, costs Hydro-Quebec only C$80 million a year, but generates revenues of about C$750 million when the utility resells it to customers in Quebec and the northeastern United States.

Michel Grignon, senior vice-president of marketing at Hydro-Quebec told Reuters that the cost to Hydro-Quebec of the Churchill Falls power is roughly C$100 million a year, and he did not dispute that the Quebec utility would sell that amount of electricity for about C$750 million.

But those revenues do not account for the cost of transmitting the energy to Quebec's power grid and onto its domestic and U.S. customers. In addition, Hydro-Quebec took all the financial and market risks associated with building the C$950 billion Churchill Falls generating facility in the early 1970s, Grignon said.

Under the contract, negotiated before the spike in world energy prices in the early 1970s, the initial price Hydro-Quebec paid for the Churchill Falls declines over time, in part because of the risks Hydro-Quebec assumed with the project.

"Since the beginning of the contract, (Churchill Falls) has made profits every year, and (had) rates of return that even Hydro-Quebec is not able to make, and this they have been making without any risk at all," Grignon said.
Grignon said Churchill Falls made C$22 million of profit last year and he expects that it will continue to be profitable for the next 30 years.

Newfoundland has also argued that the Churchill Falls contract accounts for most or all of Hydro-Quebec's annual net profit, which was C$390 million in 1995 and which the utility forecasts to rise to C$516 million next year. But Grignon said almost 9,000 megawatts of power in Hydro-Quebec's 30,435 megawatts of network capacity is produced at a cost that is lower than the price paid for Churchill Falls' power.
Those plants were built long before Churchill Falls.
"The best 9,000 megawatts that Hydro-Quebec has in its park now costs less or the equivalent of Churchill Falls -- that's production and transmission costs," Grignon said.
Hydro-Quebec pays Churchill Falls about 2.7 mils, or 2.7 tenths of a Canadian cent for each kilowatt hour. That rate is set to decline 2.5 tenths of a Canadian cent in 2001.

Grignon said Hydro-Quebec's average transmission costs are about 1.2 Canadian cents for each kilowatt hour, while the average production cost of power, excluding the electricity supplied by Churchill Falls, is about two Canadian cents a kilowatt hour.

The production cost at Hydro-Quebec's most recently commissioned megaproject, La Grande-1 in James Bay, is four Canadian cents a kilowatt hour for annual production of about 60 billion kilowatt hours, Grignon said.

Although the controversy over Churchill Falls has strong political overtones involving already strained relations between Newfoundland and the separatist Parti Quebecois government in Quebec, Grignon said the further development of hydroelectric resources in Labrador can be done in a way that both provinces benefit.

"The whole electric industry is restructuring in North America. There will be many opportunities for developing business on a win-win situation and I think that we will be able to do that," Grignon said.
